The Inca dove (Columbina inca) is a small columbid characteristic of arid and semi-arid lowlands from the southwestern United States through Central America. At an ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], which approximates the upper thermal neutral zone for this species, basal metabolic rate is considerable; maximal oxygen consumption values have been recorded at 47 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47 milliliters of oxygen per hour] and 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] for different individuals, indicating some intraspecific variation in metabolic capacity. These relatively modest rates align with the generally low energetic demand of a granivorous diet, though they are comparable to those of other similarly-sized ground doves. Hatchlings emerge from the egg at a very small size, with an initial wet weight at hatching of only 3.4 grams [Ww0 = 3.4 grams], a mass reflecting the altricial condition typical of columbid neonates. This low birth mass is followed by a period of rapid growth, fueled by intensive parental provisioning of crop milk, that quickly elevates the chick toward adult body dimensions.

For females, the ultimate wet weight achieved at adulthood is approximately 47.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 47.5 grams], a mass that places the species among the slightly larger members of the genus Columbina. Incubation of the two-egg clutch, the typical laying event for this species, proceeds at the same warm body temperature (40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]) characteristic of active metabolism. Under these thermal conditions, the eggs require a fairly abbreviated developmental period, with age at birth recorded as 14 days [ab = 14 days] of incubation at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively quick hatching interval is consistent with the species' ability to produce multiple broods across the extended breeding season. The chick then undergoes a nestling phase that culminates in the achievement of sustained flight; fledging occurs at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This early departure from the nest is typical of the genus, allowing adults to quickly initiate subsequent nesting attempts.

The onset of reproductive competence follows a period of adolescent growth and maturation. Puberty, defined by the attainment of functional gonadal activity and the capacity to breed, occurs at 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching] when the birds are maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively rapid transition to a sexually mature state is consistent with the life history strategy of a small, short-lived bird that relies on high annual fecundity to offset adult mortality. The first successful brood, however, is not initiated immediately upon reaching puberty; instead, a further delay is observed before the first breeding event. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 1.5 years since birth [tR = approximately 1.5 years since birth] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This lag of more than a year between achieving sexual maturity and actually producing the first clutch likely reflects a period of social pairing, territory acquisition, and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to sustain the metabolic demands of egg formation and incubation.

The Inca dove demonstrates a striking potential for reproductive output under favorable conditions. Females produce clutches of exactly 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt] and are capable of laying up to 4 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 4 clutches per year] when conditions of food and temperature are optimal. This capacity for serial polygamy, with rapid re-nesting following a successful fledging or a nest failure, is a hallmark of many small columbids and underpins their resilience in unpredictable arid environments. The combination of a modest clutch size with a high frequency of events yields a substantial annual reproductive output. Data from captive and field populations confirm that this rhythm of almost continuous breeding is maintained throughout the long breeding season, which in many parts of the range can extend from early spring through late autumn, only curtailed by the coldest winter months.

Longevity under natural conditions is constrained by predation, disease, and resource variability, but maximum lifespan estimates provide insight into the species' intrinsic pace of aging. Under the standard thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the oldest recorded individuals in field studies have documented a lifespan of approximately 13.3 years [am = approximately 13.3 years]. This is a considerable longevity for such a small-bodied bird, exceeding the lifespans of many passerines of equivalent mass. Such a relatively extended lifespan is life-history-consistent with the species' strategy of producing multiple small clutches each year, spreading reproductive effort across many seasons, rather than investing heavily in a single, large brood. In the context of the metabolic data reported at the same temperature, the observed lifespan suggests a moderately paced metabolic rate that, while supporting high fecundity, does not impose severe oxidative costs that would curtail survival prematurely.
